exact_claim: A Mediterranean-style eating pattern is associated with lower major cardiovascular events in high-risk adults without prior CVD.
diet_definition: Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or mixed nuts (energy-unrestricted; advice on olive oil, nuts, fruits, vegetables, fish, legumes; limited red meat, sweets)
population_definition: Adults 55-80 years at high CVD risk (type 2 diabetes or ≥3 risk factors) free of CVD at baseline; Spanish multicenter
study_type: RCT (PREDIMED; retracted 2013 version, republished 2018 after randomization protocol deviations)
comparison: MedDiet + EVOO or MedDiet + nuts vs control (advice to reduce dietary fat)
sample_size: 7447 enrolled; sensitivity analyses excluding ~1588 with protocol issues
outcome: composite of MI, stroke, or CVD death
effect_size_and_CI: HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.53-0.91) for EVOO; HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54-0.95) for nuts vs control (intention-to-treat with propensity adjustment; similar after exclusion)
errata_status: Original 2013 report retracted 2018; republished with reanalysis accounting for household and site allocation issues; results consistent
risk_of_bias: Some concerns (randomization deviations at sites/households; self-reported adherence; open-label)
quality_of_evidence: Moderate (GRADE for CVD outcomes in high-risk; supported by meta-analyses but single large trial with corrections)
limits_and_harms: No diet-related adverse events reported; energy unrestricted; not tested for weight loss as primary; adherence challenges long-term; not generalizable to low-risk or non-Mediterranean settings without adaptation
transportability: Primarily Mediterranean European ancestry high-risk adults; transportability to other ancestries, younger adults, or secondary prevention limited; dietary pattern culturally specific
app_safe_statement: Research on Mediterranean-style patterns (emphasizing olive oil, nuts, vegetables, fish, limited processed foods) has been linked to fewer major heart events in some high-risk groups without known heart disease. Discuss any pattern changes with your clinician, especially if you have other conditions or take medications.
no_personal_inference: No inference of personal CVD risk reduction or suitability for any individual based on lab flags alone.
cross_team_dependencies: Depends on lipid and glucose safety maps; ideal-weight module independent.

exact_claim: Reducing carbohydrate intake can improve glycemia in some adults with diabetes in the short term.
diet_definition: Carbohydrate-restricted eating patterns (including very low carbohydrate <26% energy); limiting processed foods as one approach
population_definition: Adults with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes (meta-analyses of RCTs)
study_type: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs
comparison: Carbohydrate-restricted vs higher-carbohydrate or control diets
sample_size: Multiple RCTs; one cited meta of 6 RCTs ≥12 months n=524 for long-term glycemic
followup: Short-term <6 months stronger; ≥12 months weaker for A1c
effect_size_and_CI: Short-term A1c benefit reported; one 12-month meta SMD -0.11 (95% CI -0.33 to 0.11) for glycemic (not significant); lipids more favorable in some analyses
primary_DOI_PMID_URL: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1)); supporting meta-analyses referenced in guideline
errata_status: None identified for primary guideline statements; individual trials vary
risk_of_bias: Low to moderate (heterogeneity in carb definition, duration, adherence, concurrent meds)
quality_of_evidence: Moderate for short-term glycemic surrogate; lower for hard outcomes and long-term
limits_and_harms: Very low-carb/ketogenic may raise LDL-C in some; contraindicated or high caution with SGLT2 inhibitors (ketoacidosis risk), pregnancy, eating disorders, kidney disease per ADA; requires medical supervision and med adjustment
transportability: Primarily studied in adults with overweight/obesity and type 2 diabetes in high-income settings; limited data in diverse ancestries, children, or advanced CKD
app_safe_statement: Some studies show short-term improvements in blood sugar measures with lower carbohydrate intake for certain adults with diabetes. Effects often lessen over time. Any change should be discussed with a clinician or dietitian, particularly if you use certain medications or have kidney issues.
no_personal_inference: No personal recommendation to restrict carbs or expectation of A1c change based on a single lab value.
cross_team_dependencies: Links to safety stop conditions for SGLT2, insulin, pregnancy, CKD, ED risk.

exact_claim: Plant-based dietary patterns and sodium restriction are suggested for people with CKD to support management of complications.
diet_definition: Higher consumption of plant-based foods (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts), lower ultraprocessed foods; protein ~0.8 g/kg/day; sodium <2 g/day
population_definition: Adults with CKD G3–G5 (not on dialysis); general healthy diverse diets
comparison: Plant-based/lower ultraprocessed vs typical; protein restriction vs higher intake
sample_size: Not a single trial; based on systematic reviews and expert consensus for practice points
outcome: Slowing progression, managing BP, potassium, phosphorus, protein waste
effect_size_and_CI: Suggestion (Level 2C) for protein 0.8 g/kg/d; practice points for plant emphasis and sodium <2 g/day; avoid high protein >1.3 g/kg/d if progression risk
primary_DOI_PMID_URL: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease (Kidney Int 2024;105(4S):S117–S314); DOI 10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018
errata_status: None major identified for diet sections as of verification
risk_of_bias: Moderate (much evidence observational or small trials; limited hard outcome RCTs for diet alone)
limits_and_harms: Protein restriction may risk malnutrition if not supervised; potassium management individualized (fruits/vegetables often encouraged initially but review with declining GFR); sodium restriction not for sodium-wasting conditions
transportability: Global guideline but evidence base mixed; cultural adaptation needed; race-free eGFR preferred
app_safe_statement: Guidelines suggest emphasizing plant-based foods, limiting highly processed items, and moderating protein and sodium for many adults with reduced kidney function. Individual needs vary widely; review with a clinician or renal dietitian.
no_personal_inference: No automatic diet prescription or assumption of CKD from a single eGFR or ACR value.
cross_team_dependencies: Depends on kidney lab flags and medication confounders (e.g., RAAS inhibitors, SGLT2).

exact_claim: Lifestyle modifications including dietary changes are foundational for managing elevated triglycerides and reducing ASCVD risk.
diet_definition: Low added sugar/refined carbohydrates/saturated fat; alcohol reduction or elimination based on TG level; weight loss 5-10%; physical activity
population_definition: Adults with hypertriglyceridemia (fasting TG ≥150 mg/dL or nonfasting ≥175); primary and secondary prevention
study_type: Guideline (ACC/AHA 2026) synthesizing trials and observational data
comparison: Lifestyle vs usual care; statin foundation for ASCVD risk reduction
sample_size: Multiple studies; TG ≥1000 mg/dL higher pancreatitis risk threshold
outcome: TG reduction, ASCVD events, pancreatitis prevention
effect_size_and_CI: Lifestyle can achieve substantial TG lowering in some; statin first-line for ASCVD; very high TG (≥1000) prioritize fat restriction to reduce pancreatitis risk
primary_DOI_PMID_URL: 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia (Circulation 2026;153:e1154–e1276; DOI 10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423); with June and September 2026 corrections
errata_status: Corrections issued June 2026 (TG threshold wording ≥150) and September 2026 (dosing table details); core recommendations stable
quality_of_evidence: Moderate for lifestyle foundation; higher for statin on hard outcomes
limits_and_harms: Severe hypertriglyceridemia requires urgent clinical evaluation (pancreatitis risk); alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes, certain meds major confounders; not all TG elevation is dietary
transportability: Applies across ancestries but Lp(a) measurement preferred over estimation; measured Lp(a) preferred
app_safe_statement: Elevated triglycerides often respond to reducing sugars, refined carbs, and alcohol, along with activity and weight management where appropriate. Very high levels need prompt medical review. Discuss any changes with your clinician.
no_personal_inference: No assumption that a lab flag means diet is the cause or that changes will normalize TG.
cross_team_dependencies: Links to lipid safety and stop conditions for severe TG.

exact_claim: Counseling on Mediterranean-style eating patterns is recommended to reduce CVD risk in people with or at risk for diabetes.
diet_definition: Mediterranean eating pattern rich in fatty fish, nuts, seeds, olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes; limited processed foods and saturated fat
population_definition: People with diabetes or at risk for diabetes
study_type: Guideline recommendation (ADA 2026) based on RCTs and meta-analyses
comparison: Mediterranean-style vs control or other patterns
sample_size: Synthesized from multiple RCTs including PREDIMED
effect_size_and_CI: Level A for CVD risk reduction; Level B for glucose metabolism
primary_DOI_PMID_URL: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Recommendation 5.30 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S89–S131)
quality_of_evidence: High for recommendation grade within ADA scope
limits_and_harms: Requires individualization; not a prescription; cultural adaptation needed
transportability: Supported across some populations but primary large trial in Spain; transportability limited
app_safe_statement: Guidelines suggest discussing Mediterranean-style eating patterns with people who have or are at risk for diabetes because of research on heart events and blood sugar measures. This is not a personal plan.
no_personal_inference: No inference that any individual will experience the average study effects.
cross_team_dependencies: Cross-links to lipid and glucose safety; independent of ideal weight.

exact_claim: Sodium intake below 2 g/day is suggested for people with CKD.
sample_size: Based on BP and progression data from trials and observational studies
limits_and_harms: Not appropriate for sodium-wasting nephropathy; individualization required
app_safe_statement: Guidelines suggest limiting sodium for many people with reduced kidney function to help manage blood pressure. Discuss amounts with your clinician.
no_personal_inference: No automatic sodium target based on a single eGFR flag.
